title: Physical Activity, Psychological Safety and Trauma-Informed Practice in Frontline Organisations
content: Background/Objectives: Trauma-informed practice emphasises psychologically safe organisational environments, yet physical activity has received limited attention within it. This study examined whether frontline organisations recognise and enable physical activity, and whether its promotion and accessibility are associated with psychological safety and other trauma-informed organisational conditions.Methods: This secondary analysis used cross-sectional data from 270 UK frontline workers (67.4% women) who completed the physical activity section of a national survey of organisational readiness for trauma-informed practice. Bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression were conducted.Results: Most participants (80.7%) reported that physical activity often or always benefited their wellbeing, yet only 38.9% reported organisational promotion and 47.0% accessible opportunities. Psychological safety was associated with promotion (Cramér’s V = 0.50) and accessibility (V = 0.37) and remained associated with promotion after adjustment (aOR = 2.12, 95% CI 1.04–4.33), although not robustly across sensitivity analyses. Trauma-informed leadership and leadership advocacy for mental health resources were robustly associated with both outcomes.Conclusions: A clear gap separated workers’ recognition of the value of physical activity from organisational enablement. Physical activity should be considered within trauma-informed workforce practice rather than framed solely as individual self-care, with psychological safety and trauma-informed leadership as potential targets for organisational intervention.
